analysis.one_liner: Bans organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and paraquat pesticides and speeds removal of pesticides banned abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the EPA to immediately stop the sale of any pesticide banned in the European Union or Canada, permanently cancel three classes of pesticides linked to brain damage in children, Parkinson's disease, and pollinator collapse, and require full disclosure of hidden 'inert' ingredients. It would also have given farmworkers new protections: bilingual labels, mandatory reporting of pesticide poisonings, fines for employers who cover up incidents, and protection from retaliation. It never advanced past its referral to the Agriculture Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, farmworkers, and rural residents exposed to pesticides would gain the most: the bill would immediately ban organophosphates (linked to neurodevelopmental damage in children), paraquat (linked to Parkinson's disease), and neonicotinoids (linked to pollinator decline). Farmworkers, who are disproportionately exposed to pesticides, would get mandatory poisoning reports, bilingual labels, whistleblower and retaliation protections, and a $25,000 reward for reporting unreported incidents. Anyone could petition the EPA to designate a dangerous pesticide and sue the EPA in court if it failed to follow the law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would immediately and permanently cancel the registration of all organophosphate pesticides, all neonicotinoid pesticides, and paraquat, and ban the sale of existing stocks [S3].

The EPA would have to immediately suspend any pesticide that the European Union, an EU country, or Canada has banned, with an expedited review in which the agency is barred from weighing economic costs [S3].

Farmworkers would gain mandatory employer reporting of pesticide poisonings (with fines of $1,000 per day and criminal penalties for cover-ups), labels printed in English and Spanish, anonymous reporting, a $25,000 reward for reporting failures, and protection from immigration action based on a report [S3].
Employees who report violations would gain whistleblower protection, including reinstatement, back pay, and damages through a Labor Department complaint process [S3].
The bill would require pesticide labels to list all 'inert' ingredients, which can make up 99% of a product and can include toxic chemicals [S3].
State and local governments would regain the power to enact their own pesticide restrictions, which federal law currently preempts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would lose the revenue from three entire product classes and from the roughly 72 pesticides the bill says are already banned in the EU [S3]. Farmers would lose access to tools they currently use, including products the bill deems dangerous by law rather than by individual EPA review, and could face higher costs or reduced yields in the transition. Any product whose registration lapses could not be sold even from existing inventory.

drawbacks.text: The bill cancels entire classes of pesticides 'by operation of law and without further proceedings,' bypassing the EPA's normal individual scientific review of each product and use — critics argue this substitutes a legislative verdict for agency science [S3].

Farmers would lose tools mid-season with no transition period: cancellations take effect on enactment, existing stocks could not be sold, and emergency exemptions would be barred for canceled pesticides [S3].

The suspension trigger is a 'may be' standard — a petition showing a pesticide may be carcinogenic, toxic, or a neurodevelopmental hazard triggers suspension if the EPA misses a 90-day deadline, a low threshold that could sweep in widely used products on contested evidence [S3].

Requiring the EPA to defer to EU and Canadian bans assumes other countries' risk assessments fit U.S. agriculture, crops, and pest pressures, and the bill forbids the agency from weighing the economic cost of a ban during review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefits are substantial and well-documented in the bill's own findings — organophosphates linked to children's brain development, paraquat to Parkinson's disease and organ failure, and neonicotinoids to pollinator collapse [S3]. The costs are real but narrower: some farmers would lose effective tools, and the bill's blunt 'deemed dangerous' approach skips the case-by-case scientific review that could distinguish high-risk uses from low-risk ones. A more gradual phase-out with transition support for farmers would have traded some speed for less disruption; this bill chose speed, betting that the health evidence justified immediate removal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with Sens. Gillibrand, Sanders, Warren, and Schatz as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
That was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action in the two years before the Congress ended [S5].
The bill had 5 cosponsors — 4 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural operations that continued using organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat for two more years are better off; farmworkers and children remain exposed to chemicals the bill would have banned.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent — 5 of 52 Senate D and I members — and no Republicans signed on; the bill also died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would immediately and permanently cancel the registrations of organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, ban sale of existing stocks, and force disclosure of inert ingredients, eliminating major product lines. Their interest in keeping these products on the market runs directly against the health protections ordinary people would gain.

Farmers would lose access to widely used pesticides with no transition period and no emergency exemptions, which could cut yields or raise costs. Some farmworker-employers would also face new reporting obligations and penalties for failing to report poisonings.
Removing organophosphates and neonicotinoids would reduce drift and residue exposure for neighboring farms and strengthen the competitive position of growers who do not rely on these chemicals.
